items.title: Emotional and Literacy Adaptation in Large Language Model–Based Medical Guidance: Development and Usability Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as conversational agents for communication and guidance, but their ability to adapt responses to a patient's emotional state and literacy level remains insufficiently characterized. In patient-facing scenarios, effective communication requires not only accurate medical content but also appropriate tone, clarity, and responsiveness to user vulnerability. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate, within a controlled, single-scenario experimental design, the ability of contemporary LLMs to adapt medical guidance responses to different levels of emotional sensitivity and literacy, and to assess their consistency in both generating and interpreting such adaptations. METHODS: A controlled benchmark was designed to evaluate how 4 LLMs adapt medical guidance responses to predefined emotional and literacy levels for a realistic patient profile asking an open-ended question. To establish a robust performance baseline, one model was deployed locally (Gemma 3 27B), and 3 are cloud-based (Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT 5.2). Each model was tested across all combinations of 5 emotional levels, 3 literacy levels, and 3 prompt-verbosity variants, yielding 45 responses per model. Generated responses were assessed against human-reviewed ground truth for emotional and literacy alignment. A separate self-evaluation procedure measured each model's ability to interpret its own outputs using the same adaptation framework. The study also examined generation-interpretation consistency and quantitative text properties, with particular attention to response length and verbosity. RESULTS: Literacy adaptation was consistently accurate across models, often achieving near-zero error, indicating strong capability in adjusting explanatory complexity. In contrast, emotional adaptation showed greater variability and was more sensitive to model architecture and prompt design. The larger cloud-based models demonstrated more stable performance overall, while the local model exhibited higher variability, particularly under shorter prompts. A systematic asymmetry was observed between generation and interpretation. The models frequently misclassified low emotional and literacy levels as "normal," suggesting limitations in recognizing user needs. Quantitative analysis revealed that response length increased with both emotional sensitivity and literacy level, with prompt verbosity and model-specific tendencies acting as secondary factors. CONCLUSIONS: Within our scenario, current LLMs demonstrated the capacity to support adaptive medical guidance, but their performance was uneven across dimensions, especially in terms of emotional generation and interpretation. For health care applications, these systems should be treated as assistive tools under human oversight rather than as autonomous communicators, with careful consideration of ethical, privacy, and safety implications in sensitive health contexts.

items.title: Empowering Preservice Language Teachers through Critical and Reflective AI Integration
items.abstract: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into education offers significant opportunities for materials development but raises pedagogical, ethical and conceptual concerns. Uncritical AI use risks producing content lacking accuracy, coherence or pedagogical relevance. Effective integration, therefore, requires content expertise, pedagogical knowledge and contextual awareness alongside technical proficiency. This chapter focuses on preservice English language teachers as a transitional cohort that is probably the last to experience materials development both with and without AI, offering insights on how RP evolves in AI-mediated contexts. Drawing on a qualitative case study of nine preservice English as a Foreign Language teachers at a state university in Turkey, the study examines how participants used ChatGPT during instructional design after receiving a technology-enhanced language teaching course for a semester. Data from interviews, observations and macroteaching post reflections reveal that while AI was initially employed to automate routine tasks, sustained engagement prompted deeper pedagogical reflection. AI-generated outputs became objects of evaluation, negotiation and revision, requiring teachers to express objectives, reassess learner needs and justify instructional decisions. Situated within technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) and emerging AI–TPACK frameworks, the findings underscore the necessity of pedagogically grounded AI training that emphasize reflective agency and teacher responsibility in AI-supported instructional design.

items.title: Enhancing brand visibility through AI-powered digital marketing: a systematic review with evidence from Vietnam
items.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI)-powered digital marketing tools, such as chatbots, recommender systems, and predictive analytics, contribute to enhancing brand visibility. Particular emphasis is placed on Vietnam, an emerging digital economy where AI adoption is uneven due to infrastructure, skills, and regulatory challenges. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, covering peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2025. Sources were drawn from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with additional screening of Vietnam-specific studies. Articles were coded thematically to synthesise insights on AI applications, branding outcomes, and contextual enablers or barriers. Findings The review shows that AI integration enhances audience segmentation, personalization, and adaptive marketing strategies, strengthening brand awareness, engagement, and recall. In Vietnam, successful adoption is facilitated by cultural localization, strategic leadership, and ecosystem partnerships. However, challenges persist around fragmented digital infrastructure, limited workforce readiness, and consumer trust in data use. Research limitations/implications The review synthesises available peer-reviewed literature up to June 2025; longitudinal and sector-specific studies are still limited. Practical implications The findings offer guidance for firms on designing culturally relevant, trust-enhancing, and resource-efficient AI strategies to improve brand visibility in emerging markets. Originality/value This study is one of the first systematic reviews to contextualise AI-driven branding within Vietnam. By bridging global advances with local market realities, it contributes both theoretical and practical insights for scholars, marketers, and policymakers.

items.title: Epistemic Justice-Aware Checklist Learning an Adaptive and Auditable Governance Framework for Bias and Fairness in Generative AI Curriculum Design
items.abstract: Generative AI increasingly participates in curriculum design, yet the resulting syllabi, learning outcomes, and assessments may reproduce subtle epistemic injustices that existing governance instruments fail to detect. We propose an adaptive and auditable framework that learns a bias and fairness checklist for generative AI curriculum artifacts rather than treating such a checklist as a static set of rules. The proposed method encodes curriculum texts into two disentangled latent subspaces, one capturing pedagogical utility and the other capturing epistemic justice violations, through a contrastive objective combined with intersectional adversarial debiasing. A psychometric utility-preserving penalty constrains this separation so that debiasing does not degrade instructional quality. Each checklist item is then evaluated by an evidential deep learning head that outputs a Dirichlet distribution over compliance states, hence yielding calibrated violation probabilities and explicit uncertainty estimates. An uncertainty-aware routing mechanism subsequently directs low-confidence drafts to a Faculty Expert Panel, whose decisions and justification notes are returned to a fine-tuning dataset. This feedback loop updates the checklist definitions and model weights iteratively, therefore allowing the governance instrument to adapt to newly identified forms of subtle bias. The main contribution is a mathematically grounded pipeline that couples representation disentanglement, evidential uncertainty quantification, and human expert feedback within a single auditable process. For curriculum governance, the framework offers transparent violation probabilities, traceable expert interventions, and a documented evolution of fairness criteria, which together support accountability in generative AI-assisted educational design.

items.title: Ergonomic interventions for treating work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder in adults
items.abstract: RATIONALE: Work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS) are disorders that develop as a result of repetitive movements, awkward postures or external forces (e.g. vibrating tools), and significantly affect the working population globally. Ergonomic interventions (which aim to enhance efficiency and comfort in the working environment) can be used to manage CANS. This review is based on a new protocol but updates part of a 2013 Cochrane review. OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness of ergonomic interventions for work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS) in adults, in terms of their effects on pain, functional status and work-related outcomes. SEARCH METHODS: We updated the 2013 review searches, searching from 31 May 2013 to 1 June 2026 in eight bibliographic databases and one trials register. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-RCTs and quasi-RCTs that evaluated single or combined ergonomic interventions (e.g. office furniture, biomechanical or ergonomic education) compared to no treatment/usual care/placebo or another active intervention (exercise/another ergonomic intervention/other treatment), or as an add-on treatment. OUTCOMES: Critical outcomes: pain, functional status (disability) and work-related outcomes (e.g. sickness absence, return to work, productivity loss at work, change of occupation). Important outcomes: global perceived effect (e.g. overall improvement), quality of life, healthcare consumption, and recurrence of injury, disorder or complaint. We prioritised outcomes in the short term (up to three months after the intervention) and were also interested in long-term results (over three months). RISK OF BIAS: We assessed the risk of bias in the studies using Cochrane's RoB 1 tool. SYNTHESIS METHODS: Two authors independently screened the search records, selected trials, extracted data and assessed risk of bias. When we judged studies to have sufficient clinical and statistical homogeneity, we performed meta-analysis. We assessed overall certainty of the evidence using GRADE for key outcomes at the short-term time point. INCLUDED STUDIES: We brought forward 13 studies from the 2013 review. We identified two new articles relating to one of those 13 studies, along with seven new studies. Therefore, in total, we included 20 studies involving 2478 participants. In 16 studies, the participants had non-specific CANS; in four studies, the participants had specific CANS (e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome). SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Results below are presented at the short-term time point. Ergonomic interventions versus no treatment, usual care or placebo in people with CANS Data were available only for trials that focused on non-specific CANS. Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in pain compared to no treatment, usual care or placebo in people with CANS (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08; 4 RCTs, 692 participants; low-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions probably result in little to no difference in functional status (disability) compared to being on a waiting list (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.34; 1 RCT (2 comparisons), 383 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in sick leave compared to no treatment (MD for continuous data -0.32, 95% CI -0.73 to 0.09; 1 RCT, 98 participants; low-certainty evidence; RR for dichotomous data 0.87, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.21; 3 RCTs, 759 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions probably result in little to no difference in recovery compared to no treatment (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.97; 1 RCT (2 comparisons), 386 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in quality of life compared to no treatment (MD 0.10, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.20; 1 RCT, 68 participants; low-certainty evidence). Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in healthcare consumption compared to no treatment when measured using continuous outcomes (MD -0.10. 95% CI -0.30 to 0.10; 1 RCT, 68 participants; low-certainty evidence), and may result in a reduction in healthcare consumption compared to usual care when measured using dichotomous outcomes (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.78; 1 RCT, 210 participants; low-certainty evidence). No data were available for recurrence of injury, disorder or complaint. Ergonomic intervention versus active intervention (exercise or another type of ergonomic intervention or other treatment) in people with CANS Data were available from trials involving participants with specific CANS and with non-specific CANS. The evidence is very uncertain about the effects of ergonomic interventions on pain (SMD 0.41, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.84; 8 RCTs, 364 participants; very-low-certainty evidence) and on functional status (disability) (SMD -0.09, 95% CI -0.85 to 0.68; 3 RCTs, 180 participants; very-low-certainty evidence) compared to active intervention in people with specific or non-specific CANS. Intense ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in recovery (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.94; 1 RCT, 257 participants; low-certainty evidence) or healthcare consumption (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.47; 1 RCT, 217 participants; low-certainty evidence) compared to ergonomic education in people with non-specific CANS. Ergonomic interventions may improve quality of life compared to exercise in people with non-specific CANS (MD -10.10, 95% CI -19.87 to -0.33; 1 RCT, 61 participants; low-certainty evidence). No data were available for work-related outcomes or recurrence of injury, disorder or complaint. Ergonomic intervention plus another treatment versus the other treatment alone in people with CANS Data were available only from trials of participants with non-specific CANS. The evidence is very uncertain about the effects of ergonomic intervention as an add-on treatment to exercise on pain (SMD -0.50, 95% CI -1.64 to 0.63; 2 RCTs, 137 participants; very-low-certainty evidence). No data were available for our other outcomes of interest. AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Overall, ergonomic interventions for work-related CANS may have no meaningful effects on pain, function, recovery, quality of life or work-related outcomes (sick leave) compared with no treatment or usual care. Findings are inconsistent for healthcare consumption. There may be a possible benefit for quality of life when ergonomic interventions are compared to exercise. The evidence for ergonomic interventions as an add-on treatment is very uncertain. High-quality, well-designed trials are needed to establish the role of ergonomic interventions in the management of CANS. items.title: Ethical and Explainable AI for Cyberbullying Detection in Education
items.abstract: The significant and complex nature of cyberbullying in educational settings is further compounded by the onset of generative AI large language models capable of generating convincing yet harmful digital content. This chapter introduces a new opportunity and addresses the limitations of recent studies that rarely handle bias, privacy, and inclusivity as interconnected issues by developing an integrated ethical framework for cyberbullying detection. The framework is built on the three pillars of bias mitigation, data privacy protection, and student inclusivity. Employing a conceptual and interdisciplinary approach, this study synthesizes findings from educational research, AI ethics, and global policy, underpinned by comparative case studies in diverse schooling environments. The chapter presents a three-pillar model and practical road map intended to guide educators, policymakers, and AI developers in deploying responsible detection systems. It further stresses the importance of using XAI to provide greater transparency and trust, resulting in safety, especially relating to digital inequalities that make many students both vulnerable users and underrepresented contributors of valuable knowledge or data for AI. The chapter provides a forward-looking approach to how responsible and explainable AI can promote safer learning environments by integrating ethical principles with practical guidance that augments protection, fairness, and inclusivity for all students.

items.title: Ethical Voice in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: When AI Participates in Decision-Making, Who Has the Right to Disagree?
items.abstract: This research paper examines the protection of ethical voice in workplaces where artificial intelligence (AI) supports or influences decisions affecting employees. It focuses on a critical human-centred question: when AI participates in recruitment, performance evaluation, task allocation, customer service, or managerial decision-making, do employees have the right and the psychological safety to understand, question, challenge, and seek correction of AI-supported decisions? The paper analyses the relationship between psychological safety, AI transparency, meaningful human oversight, and employees’ willingness to raise concerns or challenge potentially unfair or harmful automated decisions. It draws on academic literature, international governance frameworks, regulatory guidance, and documented real-world cases, including AI bias in recruitment, algorithmic grading, automated welfare fraud detection, and workplace monitoring. The study identifies major governance risks, including lack of transparency, automation bias, weak accountability, absence of safe grievance mechanisms, and insufficient human review. It proposes the Ethical Voice Model for AI Governance, based on four pillars: transparency, fairness, human oversight, and accountability and appeal. The paper concludes that protecting ethical voice is essential for responsible AI governance, workplace fairness, human dignity, and sustainable institutional trust. It provides practical recommendations for organisations, policymakers, compliance professionals, and AI governance practitioners.

items.title: Ethics and Pedagogy in AI-Driven Language Education: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Synthesis of Global Research Trends (2010–2025)
items.abstract: The aim of this paper is to provide the background for a discussion of the relationship between ethics and pedagogy in the context of environmental change and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in language education. This study scrutinized more than 150 papers and journal articles from research databases from 2010 to 2025. Results show large volumes of research activity from China, US, and UK after 2018. The rise in research activity for that period is identified in four key themes. Fewer than 20% of the articles addressed the negative aspects of AI, such as fear of student data privacy, equity, unfairness of algorithms, or other potential downsides of AI. This paper provides a balanced understanding of opportunities and challenges for AI in language education for future researchers, as well as educators and policy makers. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Language education, Ethics, Pedagogy, Systematic review, Bibliometric analysis.

items.title: Evaluating the Drivers, Barriers, and Benefits of Digital Construction Tools in the Egyptian Construction Industry
items.abstract: A digital transformation of the construction industry is now in place to improve efficiency, quality, sustainability, and competitiveness. Although numerous studies have reported the advantages of digital construction technologies, their adoption within the Egyptian construction industry remains limited. This study investigates the drivers, barriers, and perceived benefits influencing the adoption of digital construction technologies in the Egyptian construction industry. The survey was conducted with 228 construction professionals (architects, engineers, project managers) to determine how the use of digital tools such as Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), can influence the performance of the project. The results show that the main factors that prompt the use of digital include quality improvement, increased precision, and gaining a competitive edge. The main barriers found to be the most significant are the high costs, deficient infrastructure and a lack of skilled staff. In addition, the study outlines various advantages of digital tools, such as cost-saving, better quality of the project, higher safety, and higher productivity. The study will be significant to the current body of literature as it will determine the important determinants that influence the acceptance of digital technologies in the Egyptian construction sector. It provides specific suggestions on how to overcome the barriers to adoption, including building strong infrastructure, providing financial incentives and capacity-building measures. The findings can be of great use to the policymakers, practitioners, and other stakeholders in the industry that aims to accelerate digitalization and to enhance the sustainability and competitiveness of construction projects in Egypt.

items.title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies on Lecturers’ Productivity in Lagos State Owned Universities, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examined the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven research methodologies on lecturers' productivity in Lagos State University (LASU), Ojo Campus. The growing integration of AI tools such as Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and ChatGPT into academic research and teaching, alongside concerns about lecturers' research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness in Nigerian universities, motivated the study. Specifically, the study sought to ascertain lecturers' awareness of AI-driven research methodologies, examine their knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT, determine their perception of these tools in enhancing research quality and academic productivity, and establish the influence of the tools on research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, with a sample of 165 lecturers drawn from seven faculties and two schools across Lagos State Owned Universities. Data were collected using a researcher-designed instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies and Lecturers' Productivity Questionnaire (AIDRMLPQ). Out of 189 copies of the questionnaire distributed, 165 were properly completed and returned, giving a response rate of 89.2%. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) and Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between the adoption of AI-driven research methodologies and lecturers' research efficiency (r = 0.742), between knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT and academic productivity (r = 0.781), between lecturers' perception of AI tools and research quality (r = 0.766), and between AI tools utilisation and research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness (r = 0.754). The study concluded that AI-driven research methodologies play a significant and positive role in enhancing lecturers' productivity at LASU, and that institutional support and structured training remain critical to maximising the benefits of AI in higher education. It was recommended, among others, that the University organise regular training on AI tools, develop clear policies on ethical AI use, and invest in AI-compatible infrastructure to support lecturers' effective adoption of AI in research and teaching.

items.title: Evaluation of Changing Customer Behavior in the Digital Era
items.abstract: Abstract The digitalization via continuously developing artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI give the consumers the opportunity to decrease their workload and have the power to check for competitive pricing and optimized solutions. In parallel, we must recognize and embrace the essence and contribution of all digital tools providing a huge base for information connecting the consumers and business bringing speed to access data, and faster buyer–seller interactions. This in return is expected to take the consumer journey and decision-making scheme to an extended level in near future where consumers are expected to dominate more on their demands and personally defined needs not only by satisfying their personal expectations but also by giving directions to the firms’ strategies in terms of new innovations and solutions for future. This “New Customer Profile” in the digital era worths diagnosis on its changing buying roadmap compared to traditional practices as today we talk about insightful and empowered customers, increased ecommerce activities, more integration and interaction with social media, and the impact of AI use by the customers. The demand for customization requires companies to be better equipped in terms of organization, brand identity, and digital competency. Despite ongoing privacy and ethical concerns on digital arena, commodity, and retail goods expand utilizing the digital platforms reaching consumers, the complex industries such as healthcare, financial markets, and high-tech industry business still reserve room for traditional practices where in-person communication with end user and trust are highly required.

items.title: Evolução paradigmática dos fatores humanos na aviação
items.abstract: This study analyzed the paradigmatic evolution of human factors in aviation and operational safety, aiming to understand conceptual transformations related to human performance in complex sociotechnical systems. This is a qualitative, historical-epistemological, and analytical-reflective integrative review grounded in Whittemore and Knafl, Torraco, Braun and Clarke, and Levac, Colquhoun and O’Brien. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, and SciELO, as well as institutional aviation safety documents. The final corpus comprised 81 studies. Findings revealed a progressive shift from models centered on individual human error toward cognitive, organizational, systemic, and adaptive approaches. Nevertheless, limitations remain regarding fragmentation between cognition, physiology, emotion, and human-automation interaction. It is concluded that contemporary human factors require integrative models capable of understanding human performance as a dynamic and multimodal phenomenon in complex operational environments.

items.title: Evolution of the educational system and micro-psychological mechanisms: a comparative study of academic motivation and engagement in Shanghai, China and Kazakhstan
items.abstract: Introduction As noted in successive OECD assessment reports, global education systems are shifting from standardized assessments toward prioritizing students’ psychological wellbeing and autonomous agency. However, cross-cultural quantitative evidence regarding how these macro-policy transformations relate to students’ micro-psychological perceptions and academic behaviors remains limited. Methods Utilizing a cross-sectional survey, this study analyzed data from 1,309 university students in Shanghai, China, and Kazakhstan. Multi-Group Confirmatory Factor Analysis and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) were employed to examine the structural associations and measurement invariance among Perceived Educational Transformation (PET), Intrinsic Motivation (IM), and Learning Engagement (LE). Results The three-factor model demonstrated strict measurement invariance across both samples. SEM findings indicated that IM partially mediated a significant indirect associative mechanism the positive structural relationship between PET and LE (indirect effect = 0.098, 95% CI [0.076, 0.122]). This statistical mediating pathway was consistent across both cohorts, showing only trivial inter-group differences (all parameter Δ p > 0.05). Baseline comparisons revealed the Shanghai sample reported higher PET, yet IM and LE levels exhibited no significant quantitative differences between the two groups (Cohen’s d < 0.10). Discussion Higher perceptions of educational transformation do not linearly correspond to enhanced motivation, potentially constrained by unobserved systemic evaluation pressures. The findings suggest that autonomy-supportive educational environments are consistently associated with higher Intrinsic Motivation and academic engagement, regardless of differentiated macro-educational contexts. However, due to the cross-sectional design, these findings represent structural associations rather than directional causality.

items.title: Expected Confidence Benefits and Verification of AI Migration Information in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can make migration information easier to access, yet perceived confidence benefits must be distinguished from accurate advice, informed decisions and effective rights protection. This study examines that distinction using 385 adult questionnaire records from Bangladesh. It analyses five migration-information statements separately rather than treating a heterogeneous item block as a validated confidence scale. The analysis combines complete response distributions, four paired endorsement contrasts, joint response configurations and an adjusted proportional-odds model of agreement that accurate AI information could improve migration-related decision confidence. Verification against official or authoritative sources received 87.5% endorsement, compared with 64.2% for the conditional confidence proposition. Their paired difference was 23.4 percentage points, with a whole-record bootstrap 95% interval of 17.9-28.8 points. Verification exceeded endorsement of comparison benefits, the distinction between general information and legal advice, and supplementary use; all four exact paired comparisons remained below p = .001 after Holm correction. Adjusted associations with the conditional confidence outcome were imprecise: comparison benefits, migration-specific verification, the legal-advice boundary and rights-information search all had intervals spanning an odds ratio of one. The results identify a stronger stated verification norm than endorsement of several practical conditions for reliance. They do not establish actual checking, improved decision quality or a causal effect of AI services. The article develops an information-governance account in which confidence is evaluated alongside source traceability, professional referral and usable verification routes. Its contribution is a measurement-specific account of anticipated benefit and verification, with implications for migration-information design and the evaluation of AI-supported legal information.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Heart Disease Prediction: A SHAP and LIME-Based Approach — A Review
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease continues to be one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, making early and accurate risk prediction essential for timely clinical intervention. Machine learning (ML) models such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine and XGBoost have achieved high predictive accuracy for heart disease, yet their black-box nature limits clinician trust and hinders real-world adoption. This paper reviews recent research on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) applied to heart disease prediction, with a focus on two widely used model-agnostic interpretability techniques — SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations). It presents the theoretical foundations of both techniques, examines recent studies in terms of dataset, classifier, XAI method and reported performance, identifies open research gaps, and proposes an eight-phase methodology and system architecture for an XAI-based Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that predicts heart disease risk while generating transparent, feature-level explanations at both the global (population) and local (patient) level. Challenges, limitations and future research directions are also discussed. The review concludes that combining high-performing ensemble classifiers with SHAP and LIME can substantially improve the transparency, accountability and clinical usability of AI-assisted cardiovascular diagnosis.

items.abstract: Large language models and generative artificial intelligence are now significant technologies in identifying cyberbullying on online sites. In spite of the high accuracy these models have, their lack of transparency restricts trust and accountability where they are applied in the real world. The chapter focuses on the possible use of explainable generative AI in cyberbullying detection. It describes some of the most important explainability methods that can be used on large language models, compares the measures used to evaluate detection performance and explainability quality, and identifies some of the practical aspects of deploying explainable systems. The chapter highlights the relevance of explainability with respect to ethical, fair, and responsible cyberbullying detection and future research directions in the field.

items.title: Exploring AI Literacy Through a Semester-Long Course
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has raised questions about students' understanding of responsible use and academic integrity. This descriptive study examines students' experiences in a semester-long AI literacy course in a humanities program at a large public university in the United States. The course addressed AI history, capabilities and limitations, academic integrity, and ethical considerations, and provided structured opportunities to explore multiple tools. Pre-course (N = 31) and post-course (N = 25) surveys examined tool familiarity, reported use, perceived usefulness, awareness of limitations, and self-reported understanding of AI-related academic integrity. At the end of the course, respondents described more task-specific tool selection, greater attention to evaluating outputs, and increased confidence in identifying appropriate uses of AI. These findings reflect perceptions and reported practices rather than independently assessed AI literacy or ethical competence. Because the instruments differed, respondents were not individually matched, and no comparison group was included, the findings cannot establish causal improvement. The study discusses implications for AI literacy instruction in humanities and language education and for future assessment of students' AI-related knowledge and practices.

items.title: Exploring Art Appreciation Across Three Virtual Museum Configurations: Do Experience Patterns Differ by Formal Art Education?
items.abstract: This exploratory study examines how art appreciation varies across three virtual museum configurations, particularly the White Cube, Traditional Museum, and Contextualized Configurations, and whether participants’ experiential patterns differ according to their formal art education. Using a mixed-methods approach, this study integrates quantitative findings across six dimensions of aesthetic experiences with qualitative insights into the perception of composition, color, and detail. Examining the role of participants’ formal art education provides insights into how individuals with different educational backgrounds draw on perceptual, spatial, and interpretive cues. Based on these findings, the study identifies two complementary areas of design implications to support virtual art appreciation: configuration-level design considerations and participant-informed design opportunities, encompassing perpetual scaffolding, interpretive layering, analytical exploration, environmental context, and flexible flow. These implications suggest potential strategies for offering more inclusive virtual museum experiences that could accommodate different educational backgrounds and engagement preferences.

items.title: Exploring Copyright Protection for Artificial Intelligence Outputs Based on the Interaction Between Technology and Law
items.abstract: In response to the issues of whether artificial intelligence (AI) outputs can be protected by copyright, to whom the rights should belong, and how infringement should be determined, this study adopts a method combining normative analysis and historical analysis. Starting from the historical logic of copyright law’s response to technological change, it sorts out and analyzes institutional responses under the impact of printing, photography, audio and video recording, and Internet technologies, and identifies three patterns: human beings as the creative subject, a balance between empowerment and limitation of rights, and judicial action taking the lead. The study shows that generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) has the attribute of a tool, and the copyrightability of its outputs depends on the substantial intellectual control exercised by humans in prompts, parameters, selection, and revision. The degree of human contribution should be used as the standard for distinguishing weak protection from strong protection; fair use should be moderately relaxed at the training input end, substantial similarity should be strictly regulated at the output end, the burden of proof on developers should be strengthened, and judicial adjudication should comprehensively consider the responsibilities of all parties.

items.title: Federated Learning and Blockchain for Privacy-Preserving Cyberbullying Detection
items.abstract: The proliferation of generative AI has transformed cyberbullying, enabling large-scale automated harassment while creating detection opportunities. This chapter introduces a privacy-preserving framework combining federated learning and blockchain for collaborative cyberbullying detection across educational institutions without centralizing student data. Our approach addresses three critical challenges: maintaining student privacy under GDPR and FERPA regulations, ensuring transparent and accountable AI decision-making through explainable AI techniques, and establishing trust among participating institutions through blockchain-based model provenance verification. We validate our framework through experiments on combined datasets from multiple educational platforms, demonstrating 91.8 percent detection accuracy for LLM-generated harassment while maintaining differential privacy guarantees (ε=1.0). The blockchain layer successfully prevents 96.3 percent of model poisoning attacks in federated training scenarios, while SHAP-based explanations achieve 87 percent alignment with expert-annotated harassment indicators. Our work demonstrates that privacy, accountability, and effectiveness need not be competing objectives in educational AI systems, offering a practical blueprint for multi-stakeholder collaboration in combating GenAI-amplified cyberbullying.

items.title: Federated learning in cancer imaging: a comprehensive review and future outlook
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has promoted the advancement of data-driven AI medical models, bringing transformative changes to the field of traditional cancer imaging by significantly improving diagnostic accuracy. However, despite these remarkable achievements, a fundamental challenge remains: data privacy. The sensitive nature of medical data and stringent privacy regulations often limit data sharing and collaboration between institutions, hindering the development of robust and generalizable AI models. Federated learning has emerged as a promising solution to address this challenge. By enabling multiple institutions to collaboratively train artificial intelligence models without sharing their local datasets, federated learning reduces the privacy leakage risks associated with conventional centralized AI training while utilizing the collective power of diverse medical data. From 2019 to 2026, extensive research has explored the applications of federated learning in cancer imaging, demonstrating its potential to advance the field while preserving patient confidentiality. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the progress in applying federated learning to cancer imaging, highlighting key studies and their contributions. We also discuss the unique challenges facing federated learning, such as data security, data heterogeneity, and communication overhead. Finally, we explore some potential future research directions. This review aims to provide insights into the evolving role of federated learning in cancer imaging.

items.title: FinSight: An Evidence-First Financial Analysis Chatbot with Explainable Query Intelligence
items.abstract: Financial question answering is difficult because user queries often combine ambiguous intent, entity aliases, temporal scope, market data, news narratives, and advice-seeking language. Fluent responses become risky when the resolved entity, selected data sources, and evidence gaps remain hidden. This paper presents FinSight, an evidence-first financial analysis chatbot for questions about China’s financial markets. The system separates evidence production from final-response generation. Its Query Intelligence backend converts a natural-language query into explicit natural-language understanding (NLU) and retrieval artifacts, including the normalized query, product type, intents, resolved entities, source plan, retrieved documents, structured records, evidence coverage, warnings, ranking traces, and analysis summary. Downstream modules provide frontend rendering, numerical analysis, document sentiment analysis, constrained LLM-based summarization, and follow-up-question prediction. In a local evaluation of 10,000 query-style cases, including 6,236 finance-domain and 3,764 out-of-scope queries in Chinese and English, FinSight achieved finance-domain recall of 0.975, out-of-scope rejection accuracy of 0.9729, intent micro-F1 of 0.9407, topic micro-F1 of 0.9208, and retrieval Recall@10 of 0.9664. In addition, all contract checks passed in a 32-case end-to-end fuzz matrix. Typed evidence handoffs allow readers to trace each generated claim to a retrieved item or explicit warning rather than treating the final response as unsupported output.

items.title: Forecasting financial support for government institutions using artificial intelligence: The case study of museums
items.abstract: Subject. Forecasting the financial support of public institutions based on regional panel data of the constituent entities of the Russian Federation. Objectives. To develop and test a methodology for forecasting the financial support of museums using artificial intelligence methods. Methods. A panel dataset of 85 constituent entities of the Russian Federation for 2018–2024 was compiled. Machine learning methods were applied, including gradient boosting, regularized linear models, and their ensembles. Hyperparameter tuning was carried out using an artificial intelligence agent (AI agent) based on the Qwen3.5‑27B language model. Thirty‑two computational experiments were conducted. Forecast accuracy was assessed using the median absolute percentage error (MdAPE); rolling validation was applied over four test years (2021–2024). Results. The gradient boosting model achieves an MdAPE of 8.1% across regions, outperforming the best naive forecast by 1.9 percentage points and the previous‑year forecast by 4.6 percentage points. The average MdAPE under rolling validation was 12%. For 64% of the regions, the forecast error does not exceed 15%. Infrastructure‑related characteristics of institutions (28.6%) and personnel‑related characteristics (22%) demonstrate the highest predictive power. A systematic tendency to underestimate forecasts for large regions was identified; this is driven by discretionary budgetary decisions that cannot be predicted based on operational indicators. Conclusions and Relevance. Artificial intelligence methods demonstrate an advantage over traditional econometric approaches in the context of nonlinear relationships and interregional heterogeneity. The proposed methodology is applicable to forecasting financial indicators of public institutions in other sectors, provided that similar operational data at the regional level are available. The results can be used by public authorities in budget expenditure planning and in preliminary assessments of expected levels of financial support.

items.title: Forecasting LLM‐Enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted not only excitement about their usefulness for research but also concern about biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject‐matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. Most respondents expected some hypothetical LLM capabilities to increase their estimates of risk and dramatically underestimated the rate of LLM progress in those capabilities. When these capabilities arose, the median forecast did update as anticipated. The median expert initially predicted a 0.3% annual risk of a human‐caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top‐performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test, which the median expert did not expect to occur until 2030. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs already crossed this performance threshold in April 2025. A follow‐up survey conducted after these results were available found that forecasters significantly updated their median unconditional risk estimates upward, with the new median expert forecast of annual risk rising to 1.5% (as anticipated by the earlier conditional forecasts). items.title: Four large language models in parent-oriented education for pediatric flexible flatfoot: Quality, readability, hallucination, and reproducibility
items.abstract: Purpose Parents increasingly consult large language model (LLM) chatbots about pediatric flexible flatfoot, a common condition that rarely requires treatment and in which the clinical task is chiefly communication. We compared four LLMs on the quality, readability, and reproducibility of parent-oriented answers. Methods This was a cross-sectional, comparative content analysis of AI-generated text. No patients, clinical records, or human participants were involved; the units of analysis were parent-oriented questions and the chatbot responses they generated. Twenty parent-oriented questions were submitted in triplicate to ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, and Gemini in independent, memory-disabled sessions (240 responses). Two blinded pediatric orthopedic surgeons scored responses (Mika grade, four-point Likert, and a hallucination taxonomy; PEMAT-P, DISCERN, and QUEST on pooled material). Readability used five indices. Between-model differences were tested with Friedman and Dunn–Bonferroni post-hoc tests; agreement and reproducibility used intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Results All five readability indices differed between models (P < 0.001); none reached the recommended sixth-grade level. DeepSeek was most accessible (FRES 66.3) and ChatGPT least (FRES 17.7). On pooled-material instruments (inter-rater ICC 0.63–0.74), Claude scored highest for understandability (91.6%) and actionability (88.3%). Per-response clinical-quality measures were closely clustered, showed poor inter-rater agreement (ICC −0.01 to +0.07), and did not discriminate. Readability reproducibility across identical queries was moderate (FRES ICC 0.49–0.72). Conclusions Clinical-quality scales did not reliably distinguish the four LLMs, whereas readability differed substantially; none met recommended readability standards, and output was only moderately reproducible. Model choice should be guided by readability and actionability, under clinician oversight. Significance of Study For a condition managed mainly through parent education, LLM selection should rest on readability and actionability rather than presumed clinical accuracy, with output used under clinician oversight. Level of Evidence V (cross-sectional comparative content analysis of AI-generated text; no human participants).

items.title: From Advice to Emergencies: Public Perceptions of AI Support in Social Media Service Requests
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in public service delivery raises critical questions about the types of citizen requests that warrant attention and the extent to which the public trusts AI compared to human responders. This study examines safety and service related requests expressed on social media and explores public perceptions of AI and human responses to such requests. Using a mixed methods design, the study combines a qualitative content analysis of social media posts with semi-structured interviews conducted with members of the general public. The findings identify multiple categories of serviceable requests, including preventive and reassurance seeking safety concerns, guidance and escalation needs, and emergency preparedness and procedural guidance. These requests reflect how individuals use social media to seek advice, reassurance, and direction when formal public service channels are perceived as unclear, slow, or inaccessible. Interview findings further reveal that trust in AI is highly situational. Participants generally viewed AI as acceptable for low stakes, informational, and time sensitive situations, where rapid access to answers was prioritized. However, AI was largely rejected for high risk, medical, or life-threatening scenarios, where concerns about reliability, authority, and accountability were prominent. Participants consistently distinguished between the availability of AI generated responses and their perceived trustworthiness.

items.title: From AI Detection to AI Literacy-Rethinking Academic Integrity in Higher Education
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has raised concerns about academic integrity, institutional policies, and the reliability of AI detection tools. This paper examines the limitations of detection-based enforcement and argues for an approach centered on AI literacy, ethical responsibility, and critical thinking. Drawing on published studies, institutional surveys, and research findings, it discusses the widespread adoption of AI among students and educators, the risk of false accusations from detection systems, inconsistent university policies, and gaps in faculty preparedness. Particular attention is given to the challenges faced by non-native English speakers and students with limited access to digital resources. The discussion emphasizes the need to teach students how to verify AI-generated information, acknowledge AI assistance, recognize bias, and make responsible academic decisions. It also highlights the importance of faculty training, clear institutional guidelines, and assessment practices that encourage independent reasoning. items.title: From Articulation to Enforcement: District Governance of Generative AI Under Policy Ambiguity in Chicago Public Schools
items.abstract: Districts must govern generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in K–12 education without binding federal or state mandates. This study examines how Chicago Public Schools (CPS) publicly articulated a district-level GenAI governance model during 2023 to 2025, through document analysis and policy tracing. Analysis is guided by equity-anchored implementation, a construct linking implementation theory and data justice: equity commitments endure in proportion to the degree and focus of their institutional embedding. CPS articulated flexible guidance, human oversight, vendor accountability, and prohibitions on high-risk uses, alongside an articulation-enforcement gap: commitments are detailed, but monitoring, enforcement, and differentiated supports are less documented. A bounded comparison with New York City, Philadelphia, and Miami-Dade shows that institutional anchors narrow gaps only in domains they directly govern. It reframes policy ambiguity as a condition for governance articulation, distinguishes equity as harm prevention from capacity distribution, and concludes that AI governance should be judged by institutional capacity, not policy sophistication.

items.title: From Beijing to Brussels: pathways to the integration of gender in research and development (IGIRD)
items.abstract: Abstract This article offers a first consolidated historical account of the institutionalisation of the Integration of Gender in Research and Development (IGiRD). We use IGiRD as an analytical umbrella term for policies, instruments and research practices that integrate sex and gender analysis into the content, design, evaluation and governance of research and development. The article centres on how sex and gender analysis became institutionally anchored as a question of research quality, responsibility and societal relevance, while treating gender representation in research careers as a related but distinct issue. Drawing on an event-based historical reconstruction of 186 policy and institutional events from 1957 to 2024, the article traces how IGiRD developed across four partially overlapping pathways: gender equality and anti-discrimination frameworks, women’s advancement in science and technology, health and medical research, and broader integration of sex and gender analysis across research fields and governance structures. Comparing the EU, US, Canada and South Korea, the analysis shows that IGiRD has not followed a single linear trajectory. The EU pathway is distinctive because gender mainstreaming became layered onto supranational research funding and evaluation structures, while North America demonstrates strong sectoral anchoring in health and biomedical research, and South Korea illustrates rapid formal-legal anchoring with incomplete operational embedding. The article contributes to historical-institutionalist science policy research by conceptualising IGiRD institutionalisation as layered, recursive and politically reversible. Formal anchoring in laws, strategies or funding rules matters, but durable change depends on operational embedding through review expertise, guidance, training, monitoring and feedback mechanisms, and on substantive methodological integration in research practice. This perspective clarifies why IGiRD can be stabilised, narrowed or reactivated under changing political conditions and offers policy implications for strengthening gender-sensitive R&I in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence.

items.title: From benchmark to user: an end-to-end evaluation audit of an AI-based oral health screening prototype
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) for oral screening is usually judged by aggregate detection metrics on public benchmarks whose partitions, labels, and relevance to users are rarely checked. Methods We audited a prototype combining a YOLOv8m detector for six conditions (1,500 test images), a DenseNet169 histopathology network, and a ResNet18 router. Under a pre-specified plan, we measured duplication across partitions, tested removal of duplicated test images against 10,000 matched controls, compared duplicated copies' labels and predictions, compared the library versions, and ran every test image through the application pipeline. Results Near-duplicates of training images accounted for 17.3% of test and 17.1% of validation images (lower bounds). Removing duplicated test images changed mean average precision (mAP)@0.5 by +0.001 (95% confidence interval [CI] −0.012 to +0.014). Only 22% of duplicated photographs had identical labels on both copies; exploratory analysis suggested memorization of training labels in orientations seen in training. A library update moved mAP@0.5:0.95 by −0.012 with identical predictions. The router rejected 23% of in-domain photographs and 51% of photographs with ulcers, so ulcer sensitivity per image was 0.36 despite the highest benchmark recall (0.91). A class-mapping defect, still live in a public demonstration in September 2026, gave the wrong name to 73% of findings. The histopathology classifier classified every image as positive; its label was not a diagnosis. Conclusion Duplication compromised the benchmark's independence without detectably changing aggregate mAP; the defects that changed what was reported or displayed lay in the labels, evaluation software, and pipeline. Evaluations should verify partitions and labels, pin the library, and test deployed systems end to end.

items.title: From Bookkeeper to Sustainability Strategist: A Qualitative Exploration of the Evolving Role of the Accountant in the Era of AI, Sustainability and Digital Taxation in Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, sustainability reporting under IFRS S1 and S2, and digital tax administration are reshaping the accounting profession in Nigeria, yet there is little qualitative evidence on how the accountant’s role has changed or what competencies it now demands. This study explored the evolving role of the accountant in Nigeria through the lived experiences of senior practitioners. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Twenty-five senior accountants with at least 15 years of post-qualification experience in Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt were purposively selected: 5 ICAN Fellows/Professors, 6 Big 4 and mid-tier audit partners, 8 industry CFOs and 6 public sector directors. Semi-structured interviews were conducted between January and May 2025, with saturation reached at the 21st interview. Data were analysed thematically using the Braun and Clarke framework with NVivo 12, collapsing 78 codes into four themes. A four-stage evolution model emerged: Bookkeeper (1990–2005), Financial Reporter (2006–2015), Digital Analyst (2016–2023) and Sustainability and AI Strategist (2024–date). Five future-ready competency domains were identified (technical accounting, taxation, audit and assurance, sustainability reporting, and soft and ethical skills), each cited by 80%–96% of participants. The main barriers were curriculum obsolescence (88%), technophobia (72%), cost and infrastructure (68%), absence of Nigerian emission factors (64%) and regulatory uncertainty (56%). A five-pillar framework spanning regulators, professional bodies, universities, corporate organisations and individual accountants is proposed to make Nigerian accountants future-ready and globally competitive.

items.title: From Cheating to Coaching: How Chemistry Syllabi Frame Academic Integrity in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing expectations for academic integrity in higher education, yet it remains unclear how institutional AI governance is translated into course-level guidance. This study examines how academic integrity and generative AI are framed in chemistry course documents and institutional policy documents. Using a hybrid inductive–deductive qualitative document analysis, I analyzed 18 publicly available chemistry course documents and 17 institutional policy documents from nine institutions across four countries. The analysis identified five higher-order themes in chemistry course documents: consequence-focused framing of academic integrity; academic integrity framed primarily as student responsibility; boilerplate policy language dominating over contextualized integrity guidance; generative AI addressed through silence, ambiguity, or prohibition; and faculty guidance and prevention rarely being explicit. A direct comparison revealed a substantial governance gap: 15 of 17 institutional policy documents (88.2%) explicitly mentioned generative AI, compared with only 2 of 18 chemistry course documents (11.1%). Institutional policies also more frequently addressed faculty guidance, research guidance, and AI governance than course documents. These findings suggest that institutional AI governance is developing more rapidly than its translation into chemistry course-level practice. Although policies and syllabi will continue to evolve as generative AI changes, the documented governance gap provides a baseline for examining how institution-level guidance is translated into instructional practice over time. The study concludes by proposing a coaching-oriented approach that shifts syllabus guidance from primarily punitive restrictions toward transparent, ethical, and pedagogically purposeful AI use.

items.title: From Coding Assistants to Self-Healing Terminals: NeuraOS A Critical Review of AI-Driven Autonomous Command Execution and Error Recovery on Linux Systems
items.abstract: The Linux command-line interface continues to serve as the primary control surface for software development, systems administration, and cloud operations, yet it executes instructions syntactically, without semantic awareness of user intent and without built-in mechanisms for diagnosing or repairing runtime failures. Over roughly the last decade, three largely distinct research communities have each addressed part of this problem: large language model (LLM)-based coding assistants embedded in integrated development environments (IDEs), natural-language-to-command translation systems that lower the barrier to shell usage, and operating-systems research on self-healing and autonomic computing that targets distributed and cloud infrastructure rather than the interactive terminal. This paper presents a structured, critical review of these three strands, together with the log-based anomaly-detection and AIOps literature that supplies much of the diagnostic machinery such systems would require. Literature was retained where it addressed semantic command interpretation, real-time or near-real-time failure diagnosis, autonomous or semi-autonomous recovery, or persistence of prior failure-resolution experience. The reviewed work is organized along four analytical dimensions — runtime integration, autonomy level, diagnostic depth, and knowledge retention — and compared qualitatively across these dimensions. The synthesis shows that autonomy and diagnostic sophistication increase substantially when moving from IDE assistants toward self-healing infrastructure research, but this increase is accompanied by a shift away from the single-operator, single-machine terminal context, and that no reviewed system combines real-time in-terminal diagnosis, multi-pathway recovery, and durable per-machine experiential learning while remaining confined to user space. The review further discusses recurring safety and governance themes — confidence-gated autonomy, privilege-aware execution, and explanation-first human oversight — that constrain the design space for any terminal-level orchestration layer, and it identifies four concrete research gaps together with a near-, mid-, and long-term research roadmap. The review does not claim that any single technology described is either novel or previously unstudied in isolation; its contribution is the cross-domain synthesis and the identification of the specific combination of properties that remains unaddressed.

items.title: From Culturally Grounded Virtual Games to Real-World Destination Engagement: Flow, Cultural Identity and Behavioral Intention Conversion
items.abstract: Culturally embedded virtual games increasingly shape digital design, cultural communication, and place experience, yet how immersion translates into real-world engagement remains unclear. Drawing on the cognition–affect–conation model and flow theory, this study analyzes survey data from 458 young players. Presence, perceived realism, and curiosity significantly enhance emotional interaction and flow, while challenge improves flow but not emotional interaction. Flow mediates the relationship between virtual cultural experience and intention to visit real-world places; emotional interaction has no direct effect. Cultural identity strengthens the flow–participation relationship, highlighting its role in converting virtual immersion into cultural engagement. Culturally grounded games therefore function as destination pre-experience and cultural design platforms, through which digital scenes, cultural symbols, and interaction shape players’ imagination, identification, and willingness to participate in real-world cultural spaces. Findings inform game design, heritage communication, and place-experience design.

items.title: From goal framing to participation experience: a cognitive-affective process perspective on mass participation sport events
items.abstract: Purpose This study opens the “psychological black box” of participation experiences in mass participation sport events (MPSEs) by examining how goal frames are associated with experiential outcomes through cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. Drawing on goal-framing theory and the cognitive-affective processing system (CAPS), it proposes a process model linking goal frames to participation experiences, with social connectedness as a boundary condition. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey was conducted with participants in Taiwan who had engaged in non-elite sport events within the past year (N = 405). Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with bootstrapping, employing established scales to measure goal framing, cognitive engagement, psychological empowerment, event enjoyment, subjective vitality, and social connectedness. Findings All three goal frames were positively associated with cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. Cognitive engagement was positively associated with both event enjoyment and subjective vitality, whereas psychological empowerment was positively associated with subjective vitality but not event enjoyment. Social connectedness significantly moderated the relationship between psychological empowerment and subjective vitality, while the other moderation effects were not statistically significant. The indirect effects further revealed two distinct pathways, with cognitive engagement operating across both experiential outcomes and psychological empowerment being associated with subjective vitality. Originality/value This study advances a process-based perspective by integrating goal-framing theory with CAPS to explain how goal frames are associated with experiential outcomes through cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. It demonstrates that social connectedness functions as a selective rather than universal boundary condition.

items.title: From Goals to Results: An Analytical Perspective on Three Global Challenges Through the Lens of Project Management
items.abstract: This independent analytical paper examines three major global challenges: biodiversity protection, the future of work in the age of artificial intelligence, and global supply chain resilience. Through the lens of project management, the paper explores the gap between global commitments and effective implementation, the unequal distribution of opportunities and resources, and the importance of accountability, education, and human empowerment. It argues that meaningful progress should be measured not only by stated goals, technological advances, or economic indicators, but also by tangible and lasting improvements in people's lives and opportunities. The paper reflects the author's personal perspective and applies project management principles to the analysis of complex global challenges.

items.title: From Hazard Maps to Decision Intelligence: A Critical Review of GIS, Remote Sensing and GeoAI for Disaster Risk Management and Engineering Resilience
items.abstract: Disaster risk is inherently spatial, yet geographic information systems (GIS) are still frequently used to end analysis at a classified hazard map rather than to support an engineering or operational decision. This critical review traces how GIS, integrated with remote sensing (RS), multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), Web-GIS and geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI), has evolved across the disaster management cycle, and evaluates whether the resulting products are validated, uncertainty-aware and usable in civil-engineering practice. Twenty foundational studies (1992–2017) covering general emergency management, floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones and coastal hazards, drought and forest fire are appraised against a structured set of dimensions and are updated with recent systematic reviews of Web-GIS, AI/ML-enabled GIS, drone-based hazard sensing and AI-based landslide analysis. Four analytical families (knowledge-driven, data-driven, simulation-based and integrated Web-GIS/GeoAI) are compared. Knowledge-driven methods such as AHP and weighted overlay remain valuable where event inventories are scarce but are sensitive to expert-assigned weights; statistical and machine-learning models can improve prediction but are vulnerable to spatial leakage, non-representative inventories and limited interpretability; operational Web-GIS and GeoAI systems are advancing quickly but are rarely validated against independent events or evaluated by their effect on decisions. The most persistent gap is the translation of hazard classes into engineering quantities such as flood depth and velocity, design ground motion, slope safety factors, damage states and lifeline reliability. The review proposes (i) an eight-stage data-to-decision framework linking GIS, RS, GeoAI and engineering analysis, (ii) a minimum reporting and validation checklist for GIS-based hazard studies, and (iii) a prioritised research agenda covering multi-hazard modelling, near-real-time Web-GIS, uncertainty-aware GeoAI, digital twins, BIM–GIS integration and decision-centric validation.

items.title: From Legal Pads to Artificial Intelligence: How Technology Has Changed the Work of the Preacher—and What Must Never Change
items.abstract: Description Artificial intelligence is changing how people research, write, and communicate, raising important questions for the church and the work of the preacher. How can pastors benefit from emerging technologies without surrendering the personal study, prayer, theological judgment, and spiritual responsibility essential to faithful preaching? In From Legal Pads to Artificial Intelligence: How Technology Has Changed the Work of the Preacher—and What Must Never Change, Brent Madaris, D.Min., examines the relationship between technological assistance and the preacher’s personal responsibility in sermon preparation. Drawing on pastoral ministry, theological study, and professional experience in healthcare, the author considers both the potential benefits and the limitations of artificial intelligence in vocational ministry. The essay distinguishes between using AI as a tool for research, organization, and refinement and allowing it to substitute for the preacher’s own biblical study, spiritual reflection, theological discernment, and pastoral judgment. It also considers how lessons from the responsible use of AI in clinical practice may inform discussions about its use in ministry. Rather than offering an unqualified endorsement or rejection of artificial intelligence, this work argues for thoughtful and responsible engagement with emerging technology while maintaining the convictions and practices that must remain central to Christian preaching. AI may assist in preparing a sermon, but it cannot prepare the preacher. This essay is intended for pastors, ministry leaders, theological educators, students, and others interested in preaching, Christian ministry, theological reflection, and the ethical use of artificial intelligence. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; sermon preparation; preaching; pastoral ministry; Christian ministry; theological education; Christian ethics; technology and religion; responsible AI use.

items.title: From Operating Procedures to Verified Critical Controls: A Risk-Assessment Framework for Mobile Equipment in Opencast Mines
items.abstract: Dumper, tipper and haul-truck operations in opencast mines expose workers to high-consequence hazards arising from vehicle mass, restricted visibility, mixed traffic, changing haul roads, dumping edges and human performance. This study develops an implementable risk-assessment framework that translates Indian mine-safety requirements and international evidence into operational controls and verification routines. A purposive integrative review of official DGMS, MSHA and NIOSH material and peer-reviewed research was combined with examination of the supplied risk-assessment-based safe operating procedure. The search was not systematic, and no incident-level dataset or formal quality appraisal was available. Sources were mapped to operating phase, hazard, control, verification, accountable role and learning indicator. The proposed framework covers six operating phases and six control domains. It assigns task HIRA to baseline screening, JSA/JHA to detailed high-risk steps, Bowtie to fatal-event pathways and critical controls, and FMEA/FMECA to equipment failure modes. It also specifies five verification modes and links critical controls to failure responses, owners and prospective indicators. The framework is sufficiently specified for site adaptation and prospective pilot evaluation; it has not been tested as an intervention or empirically validated.

items.title: From Personalization to Manipulation: A Systematic Review of Ethical Issues of AI and its Impact on Young Users Through Social Media
items.abstract: This systematic review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) shapes the digital experiences of young users through social media reels and personalized content. The study focuses on the ethical dimensions of these developments, addressing concerns such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, exposure to potentially harmful content, and the broader psychological effects on adolescents. This paper evaluates current literature to uncover the ethical tensions between personalization and manipulation. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, this review systematically analysed 42 peer-reviewed articles and industry reports published between 2015 and 2024. The analysis highlights how AI's profit-driven logic reinforces compulsive behaviours, body image concerns, and social comparison among adolescents. Such effects are particularly pronounced among adolescents, who are in a critical stage of identity formation and are more vulnerable to the psychological consequences of digital exposure. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a multi-stakeholder ethical framework designed to promote algorithmic transparency, empower young users through digital literacy, and enhance regulatory accountability. This framework emphasizes the shared responsibility of technology companies, policymakers, educators, and guardians in mitigating the adverse impacts of AI-driven personalization. The review's insights hold significant relevance for those seeking to balance innovation with ethical safeguards in the evolving landscape of youth, technology, and social media.

items.title: From Prediction to Interaction: A Behavioral Informatics Framework for AI in Preventive Health
items.abstract: Abstract In this viewpoint, we present our perspective—informed by published evidence and by our own work on AI-driven digital health systems—on why AI has had limited real-world impact in preventive health and how it should be redesigned. Most AI systems in health care are built as episodic prediction tools, whereas preventive care depends on sustained behavioral change; the consequences are visible in consistently high attrition and low long-term adherence across digital health interventions. The aim of this viewpoint is to argue that this failure is structural rather than incremental and to propose an integrated, interaction-centric alternative. We advance 3 key messages. First, the limited impact of AI in preventive health reflects a structural misalignment between episodic, prediction-centric system design and the longitudinal dynamics of health behavior. Second, addressing this misalignment requires treating continuous interaction as the primary unit of design, which we articulate through a behavioral informatics framework integrating 6 interdependent layers: data, knowledge, reasoning, interaction, behavior, and governance. The contribution of this framework is explicitly integrative: it synthesizes previously separate strands, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, behavioral intervention technologies, and human-AI interaction research, into a single system-level account. Third, evaluation must shift from predictive accuracy and short-term engagement toward measurable behavioral trajectories and longitudinal outcomes, with explicit attention to feasibility and to conditions under which simpler, non-AI interventions remain preferable. This viewpoint is addressed to digital health researchers and AI developers, behavioral scientists, clinicians involved in preventive care, and policymakers responsible for governing continuously interacting AI systems.
